blocks.h: Why does `mid` stay put after swapping with `hi`?
p: The value swapped in from `hi` has not been inspected; it could be a 0, 1 or 2. `mid` must look at it before moving on. After swapping with `lo` the opposite holds: everything in `[lo, mid)` is already 1s, so the value that arrives at `mid` is a known 1 and `mid` can advance.

p: `nums = [1,2,3]`. Each call records its current path immediately:

blocks.h: Why record at every node, not only at the leaves?
p: A subset does not have to be 'complete': `[1]` and `[1,2]` are both valid. The recursion tree has one node per subset, so there are 2ⁿ of them (8 here). Subset-problems record at each node; permutation-problems record only at depth n.

blocks.h: Why does equality at both ends break the plain version?
p: Take `[1,0,1,1,1]`: `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` is true, yet the left half `[1,0,1]` is not sorted, so the range test would go wrong. bullets: Time: O(log n) typical, O(n) worst case, e.g. an array of all equal values with the target missing, where each step removes only two items.
Space: O(1).

81.takeaway: Rotated-array binary search where duplicates can hide the sorted half: when lo, mid and hi are equal, shrink by one on each side.

blocks.h: Why does a bar get popped exactly when a lower bar arrives?
p: For the bar at the top, the new lower bar `h` is its nearest smaller bar on the right, and the new top of the stack is its nearest smaller on the left (stack heights increase, so everything between them is at least as tall). The rectangle with that bar as the limiting height therefore spans exactly `i - left - 1` bars, and its area is final the moment it is popped.

bullets: Time: O(n). Each index is pushed once and popped once.
Space: O(n) for the stack.

84.takeaway: Monotonic increasing stack: each bar's maximal rectangle is computed when a shorter bar pops it.

What it does

p: `s = "25525511135"`. The recursion reaches four parts 43 times; 2 of those use every digit (shown), and the other 41 leave digits over and are dead ends. Branches with an invalid segment such as `"256"` or `"01"` are cut earlier.

blocks.h: Why is `break` correct but `continue` for the other checks?
p: Running out of characters affects every larger size too, so `break` ends the loop. A leading zero or a value over 255 only rules out that size; a different size may still work, hence `continue`. (`'0'` is fine, but `'05'` is not, and `'256'` fails while `'25'` passes.)

bullets: Time: O(1) in effect: at most 3⁴ = 81 segmentations, each costing a constant amount of work.
Space: O(1) depth (4 levels).

93.takeaway: Backtrack over 1–3 digit segments with leading-zero and range checks; exactly four parts must consume the whole string.

What it does

blocks.h: Why does this count BSTs and not all binary trees?
p: For a BST on values 1..k with root r, the BST property forces the smaller r−1 values left and the larger k−r right, so only the *shape* of each side is free. The count depends only on the sizes, which is why a 1-D table indexed by node count is enough. This is the Catalan recurrence: 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, …

bullets: Time: O(n²), two nested loops.
Space: O(n) for dp.

96.takeaway: Count BSTs with the Catalan recurrence: sum over each root of left-count × right-count.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Carry the level along with the node
BFS visits nodes in nondecreasing depth
A leaf is the only thing that ends a root-to-leaf path
First leaf found by BFS is at the minimum depth

blocks.h: Why BFS and not DFS here?
p: DFS must explore the whole tree before it knows the minimum, because a deep leaf on one side tells nothing about a shallow leaf on the other. BFS visits level by level, so the first leaf it meets is guaranteed to be the shallowest, and it stops there. The worst case is the same O(n), but BFS often finishes early.

bullets: Time: O(n) worst case.
Space: O(w) for the queue (up to O(n) for a wide tree).

p: A node with only one child is not a leaf. Checking `not node.left or not node.right` would stop one level too early, e.g. on `[2,null,3]`, where the answer is 2, not 1.

111.takeaway: Minimum depth is a BFS stop-at-first-leaf; remember that a node with one child is not a leaf.

Finds the rightmost node of the left subtree, which is the last node visited in preorder inside it
The predecessor in a Morris-style traversal

p: Tree `[1,2,5,3,4,null,6]`. Notation `v(left,right)`; an empty slot means no child. A node with no left child needs no change.

blocks.h: Why does this give preorder order?
p: Preorder is node, left subtree, right subtree. Moving the left subtree into the right slot and attaching the old right subtree after the left subtree's last node produces exactly that sequence along the right spine. Each node only needs its own left subtree handled, because later steps handle the nodes inside it.

bullets: Time: O(n) amortized. The inner `while` only walks a left subtree's right spine, and those nodes end up on the main right spine that the outer loop walks once.
Space: O(1), no recursion or stack.

114.takeaway: Flatten in place: for each node, attach its right subtree to the rightmost node of its left subtree, then shift left to right.

Building the next level in order

blocks.h: Why does this work when the tree is not perfect?
p: A perfect tree lets you use `node.left.next = node.right` and `node.right.next = node.next.left`. In a general tree some children are missing, so those shortcuts break. Building the whole next level as a plain list and linking neighbours does not care which children exist; null children are filtered by `if c`.

bullets: Time: O(n), each node appears in one level list.
Space: O(w) for the level lists, not O(1). A pointer-only solution that walks the already-built `next` chain gets O(1) extra space, which is the follow-up interviewers ask.

117.takeaway: Level lists make 'next right' trivial for any tree shape; the O(1)-space follow-up walks the next-pointers of the level above.

p: `[[2],[3,4],[6,5,7],[4,1,8,3]]`. `dp` holds the minimum cost from each cell to the bottom:

Going bottom-up means each row has one more entry than the row above, so `dp[i]` and `dp[i+1]` always exist and the answer ends in a single cell, `dp[0]`. Top-down needs boundary handling for the edges and an extra step to take the minimum over the last row. Space: O(n), one row.

p: `[3,3,5,0,0,3,1,4]`. Each row is the state after processing that day's price.

blocks.h: Why can the four updates be done in this order within one day?
p: Each line reads the value just updated on the line above, so the same price may be used for a sell and a following buy on the same day. That is harmless: it means 'sell and re-buy today', and it can only equal or improve a state, never fabricate profit (selling and buying the same day nets zero).

bullets: Time: O(n), one pass.
Space: O(1), four variables instead of a 2-D table; the table form is dp[day][transactions][holding].

p: `hit → cog` with `[hot,dot,dog,lot,log,cog]`. Each BFS layer maps next words to the set of layer words that reach them:
bullets: Backtracking from `cog` through the parents gives 2 shortest paths: hit→hot→dot→dog→cog, hit→hot→lot→log→cog.

blocks.h: Why remove `level` from `words` before expanding, not right when each word is discovered?
p: Two words in the same layer can both reach the same next word, and both must be recorded as parents. If the next word were deleted the moment it was first discovered, the second parent would be lost. Removing the whole previous layer at the start of the next round forbids going backwards or sideways while still letting same-layer parents accumulate.
BFS processes whole layers, so when `endWord` shows up every shortest path has the same length and all its parents were recorded in that layer. Continuing would only add longer paths.

bullets: Time: BFS is O(N · L · 26) for N words of length L; the output can be exponentially large in the worst case, so path reconstruction can dominate.
Space: O(N · L) for the sets and parent map.

126.takeaway: Word Ladder II: layered BFS that stores all parents, then DFS backwards from the end word to list every shortest path.
